Yowamushi Pedal: Resonance Pedaism

弱虫ペダル レゾナンス・ペダイズム — Training sim × bicycle road racing (anime IP)

RoleLead Game Designer · PM

How I ran production

  • Team: 8 game design, 7 engineering, 4 art, 2 UI, 2 QA, 1 sound, 1 marketing, plus outsourced partners. Daily stand-ups, weekly syncs, milestone reviews.
  • Plan: benchmark reverse-engineering → alpha → beta 1 → beta 2 → closed beta, tracked in Redmine, Google Sheets, Cacoo and AI agents.
  • Scope call: after alpha, building everything for launch — Guild vs Guild included — would have sunk the schedule. I cut GvG from launch and shipped it two weeks later: players explore PvE and PvP first, then compete harder, the same pacing our benchmarks and competitors use.
  • Product call: test plays showed we were too close to our benchmarks, so we added new mechanics to make the game its own — worth the extra time.
  • Live-ops fix: D30 sat at 7% against a 10–15% target. Players weren't out of content — late-game RNG made their training and purchases feel meaningless. I rebalanced RNG to matter most in evenly matched races and fade as the power gap grows, backed by win-back campaigns. D30 rose to 9–10%.

What I designed

  • Owned the two core features — training simulation and race animation — from benchmark research and GDD to UI wireframes and shipped build.
  • Level design linking trained parameters and skills to race outcomes; balanced IAP packs and gacha lineups.
  • Built the milestones and the post-launch operation calendar; led the design team through launch into live ops.

Process highlight

  • Specced the training loop as a turn economy: five exercises feed five parameters, while goal, sub-goal and condition all compete for the same limited turns.
  • Benchmarked Uma Musume: Pretty Derby and Blue Lock: Project World Champion, then decided which parameters drive stamina, speed and skill activation in a race. (Mapping under NDA.)
  • Built an interaction legend into the wireframe — interactable / non-interactable / special boost — so UI, engineering and art read priority straight off the spec.
  • Layout rule: everything one decision needs is visible without a tap; only depth sits behind a button.
  • Between test plays: cut the training cycle by two-thirds and retuned goals — players were dropping out before the payoff. Faster progression let them discover more content. D1 retention rose from 44% to 73%.
  • Wireframe → final: moved the race button so players stay on training until ready, and merged skill purchase into the skill-point display to cut competing controls.

03/2025 · Prototype

Light Escape — solo 4-hour prototype

RoleSolo — design & build
EngineUnity
Time box4 hours
Round5-minute survival

What I designed

  • Picked the constraint first: one light zone alive at a time, so safety is temporary and the player can never settle. Every other rule serves that one.
  • Wrote difficulty as numbers: light cycle 10s → 3s over 180s, ghost 2.5 → 5.5 m/s against a 6.0 sprint, stamina making sprint a spend — early game survivable on reflex, late game only by planning.
  • Split each cycle 70/30 into stable and warning phases, so difficulty lives in when the player commits, not in guessing where to run.
  • Removed unfair losses: nothing starts until the player reaches the first light, and a loss needs 0.3s of continuous contact — a graze is not a death.
  • Scoped it to 4 hours solo: one room, no NavMesh, placeholder assets. Choosing what to cut was the exercise.

Quality & IP Management

品質管理

“Doesn't look like them.” “Old-fashioned.” “Not attractive.” — vague IP feedback stalls art for weeks. I wrote a review standard that turns it into criteria art and the IP holder can check at rough stage.

Gacha illustration quality standard

  • Four gates, not a score: identity (it's really them), character (it's like them), ownership (“I want this one”), modern appeal (holds up next to today's top gacha). A card passes only when all four do.
  • “Similar” made checkable: face shape, eyes, fringe, silhouette, build, expression, posture — shape match + acting match.
  • “Modern” made relative: keep the IP's character design, update camera, light, depth and eye flow against a benchmark set refreshed every quarter.
  • “Attractive” made a spec: each order carries one sentence defining the moment fans will want to own.
  • Agreed through meetings with the IP holder — approvals stopped blocking releases. Written with AI assistance for structure and Japanese review.

AI in My Workflow

AI活用

I build AI agents for my team, because how fast a team iterates matters as much as what it ships.

Quality

A daily bug-check agent scans master data and code against the operation schedule. QA's routine check dropped to under 10 minutes a day, freeing them for functional and event testing.

Master data

An agent reads level-design docs — rates, rewards, quantities — and enters the data itself. We only review. Doc-to-data mismatches went to zero.

Docs & planning

Project agents keep every GDD and level-design doc on one format and rule set, so documents never contradict each other. They also review docs, draft event schedules, progress reports and meeting notes, and polish JP business correspondence with the IP holder.

Game Teardown

ゲーム分析

Blue Lock: Project World Champion — why it works, where it loses players, and what I'd change as its producer.

What works

Character design and VFX make every player look like a star. The spectacle is the reason to pull, and it lands.

What breaks

The UX isn't friendly to new players. As a player I couldn't tell where exchange items come from, how the championship works, or how to enter it.

What I'd change

  • A “where to get” link on every exchange item.
  • A guided first championship with a clear entry flow.
  • Track drop-off on those screens to confirm the fix.

About

自己紹介

I came to games from an unusual road — a Japanese Law degree, then language school in Japan. Law taught me to read dense material closely, find the rule underneath it, and argue from evidence rather than instinct — the same muscle behind benchmark research, GDD writing, and reading KPI data before touching a number.

Every genre I've shipped in — match puzzle, action RPG, training sim — I learned from zero. Breaking an unfamiliar domain down and turning it into a spec other people can build from is what I do fastest. Japanese, Vietnamese and English are how I gather that information, not the whole of what I bring.

Five years at enish took me from operating events on a 9.2M-download puzzle game to leading a 26-person team on a new IP title from concept through launch and live ops.

I play widely, too — 348 hours in Umamusume: Pretty Derby, plus Blue Lock: Project World Champion, Dark War Survival, Arena of Valor, Cult of the Lamb, Sea of Stars, Little Nightmares, God of War, The Last of Us and Horizon.

Long-term goal: to ship a game the world knows as made in Vietnam, led by a woman.
